prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and financial frictions amplify and propagate shocks, and for building the analytical framework for credit cycles and macro-financial fluctuations

statement.case_for: B006 has the cleanest combination of conceptual centrality, durability and breadth of the top candidates. Kiyotaki-Moore gave macroeconomics a tractable mechanism in which asset prices and collateral constraints feed on each other, so small shocks become large and persistent fluctuations. The financial-accelerator and intermediary-frictions work, with Gertler as the main developer, turned the mechanism into a quantitative and policy-usable framework. This is now the standard way to model credit in business-cycle, crisis and macroprudential analysis. The core papers are nearly three decades old, so the ideas have had time to be tested, extended and stress-tested by 2007-09. The framework is also the foundation on which later heterogeneous-agent and household-balance-sheet work was built. The discovery is a single coherent mechanism with a clear originating pair and a clearly related third contributor, which is easier to defend than the bundled or crowded alternatives.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and overlap. Bernanke's 2022 prize recognised the banking and financial-crisis side, and the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator line cannot be recognised again. That makes Gertler's share harder to separate from work already honoured, and it argues for a two-name award (Kiyotaki and Moore). Gilchrist's empirical contribution is also left out. Empirical identification of the collateral channel is mixed, and some may judge the mechanism to be better established as theory than as measured fact. Gertler also appears on the New Keynesian ballot, so credit could be split or double-counted across candidates.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first but proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore, arguing that the collateral-constraint mechanism is the clean origin. He thinks Gertler's accelerator work builds on Bernanke-Gertler, which the 2022 prize already partly recognised.
responses.response: The point is fair and I have not dismissed it. The two-name award is the most defensible attribution of the credit-cycle mechanism itself. I still include Gertler because his contribution is not only the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator. His later work with Kiyotaki and others on intermediary frictions is a distinct, post-Bernanke extension that turned the mechanism into a quantitative framework for crises and policy. I therefore see the third name as an open question for the committee, not a settled one. If the committee concludes that Gertler's marginal credit is too entangled with Bernanke's prize, I would accept the pair and would not hold up the award on that point.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B006 first, with B047 second. He argues that BLP and the dynamic industry models transformed empirical IO and are well confirmed, and that the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes trio is clean.
responses.response: I agree that B047 has a strong claim and a clean trio, and I ranked it second for the same reasons. The difference for me is breadth of use across fields. Collateral and financial-friction mechanisms are now part of the shared core of macro, finance and policy modelling. BLP is a methodological toolkit whose impact is concentrated in IO, antitrust and adjacent applied fields. I would not call that a decisive scientific difference, and I do not treat the number of members who rank B047 first as evidence of merit. The part of the B047 case I would press is the omission of Bresnahan and Reiss, which a three-name cap forces. That is an attribution cost B006 does not carry to the same degree. For that reason I keep B047 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B023 first. He argues that the task-based and skill-biased account of technology and the China-shock evidence changed how both economists and policymakers understand inequality, with large cross-field influence, and he notes the three-name cap leaves out Dorn.
responses.response: I agree that B023 has very large influence and credible empirical designs, and I rank it third. My reservation is the one Boppart also names: the bundle joins two strands (technology and wage structure; trade shocks) with partly different originators, and the credit overlaps with already-recognised work by Goldin-Katz and Acemoglu. Any three names leave out someone with a strong claim, most obviously Dorn. The trade-shock magnitudes are still debated. I do not think these points defeat the candidate. They do make the unit of recognition less sharp than a single mechanism such as B006. If the committee prefers B023, I would favour a version that stays within one of the two strands, to keep the citation precise.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B047 first and proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore on B006, rating it fourth. He cites overlap with the 2022 prize and Bernanke's earlier recognition, and mixed evidence on the collateral channel.
responses.response: The empirical point is the one I take most seriously. Direct identification of collateral channels is difficult, and the evidence is more mixed than the theory's influence suggests. My reply is that the contribution is mainly conceptual: it supplied the amplification mechanism that later empirical and quantitative work then tested in many settings. A mechanism need not be settled in every empirical detail to be prize-worthy, provided it organised a large research programme and survived the major test of the 2008 crisis. I agree that the 2022 overlap is a real concern and not a cosmetic one, and I would answer it by keeping the citation anchored in the collateral-constraint and credit-cycle mechanism, not the banking-crisis theory.

uncertainties: Whether Gertler's marginal credit is separable from the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator that the 2022 prize already touched, which decides between a two-name and a three-name award.
How much weight the committee gives to thematic overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
Whether Gertler's presence on the New Keynesian ballot (B048) should affect how his contribution is credited here.
My assessment of influence and citation record rests on general knowledge, and I have not independently verified it.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows long-term co-authorship with John Hassler (chair) and co-authorship with Timo Boppart (co-opted member); both have given opening views on these candidates, and I disclose this without adjudicating it. I am also a long-term co-author of Giovanni Violante, who is credited on B043. That ballot is not part of my preferred configuration or alternatives. None of the credited names on B006, B047 or B023 appears among my listed co-authors, so no recusal-relevant connection to my preferred candidates is apparent from the supplied profile. My own field is heterogeneous-agent macro, which is adjacent to B006, and I have tried to apply the same criteria as for other fields.
